When examining the influence of differently oriented 2.5D convolutions in axial, coronal, and sagittal views, results in [Table 6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8515181/#T6) illustrated that in our experiments, the models trained in axial view provide more accurate segmentation in enhancing tumor and tumor core regions. This was predictable since most MRI image acquisitions are obtained with a higher resolution in the axial direction. On the other hand, the models trained in the sagittal view generated a better segmentation of the whole tumor. This is possibly due to the greater volume of the target region, for which the more global information contained in the dimension of lower resolution is more relevant. 2.5D Multi-View Inception modules can be implemented in any architecture and benefit the accuracy of the segmentation. It would also be interesting to assess this block using dilated convolutions instead of using different kernel sizes.

[Tables 3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8515181/#T3), [4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8515181/#T4) compare our results with the first and second-ranked models in the BraTS 2018 and 2019 challenge. All top-performing methods have in common the use of U-Net like architectures, and all of them used fusing strategies like an ensemble of models.

In the 2018 BraTS challenge, the first-place competitor ( [21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8515181/#B21)) proposed a variational autoencoder branch for an encoder/decoder model to reconstruct the input image simultaneously with segmentation. The second place used an ensemble of 10 3D U-Net with minor modification models and implemented a co-training strategy using additional labeled images. We also compared our results with the cascade network in addition to test time augmentation (TTA) and a conditional random field for post-processing, implemented by ( [51](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8515181/#B51)). TTA is a data augmentation technique, such as spatial transformations, but applied at test time to obtain _N_ different segmentation results combined to get the final prediction.

In terms of optimization in the 2019 BraTS challenge, the first and second place used warming up learning and multi-task learning strategies. The second-place submission of Zhao et al. ( [15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8515181/#B15)) started from a base model that consists of a U-Net architecture with dense blocks joined with a self-ensemble module that combines predictions made at different scales of U-Net to obtain the final prediction. Additional strategies are then applied to improve performance, including random patch-size training, semi-supervised learning, warming up, and multi-task learning. The authors made an ablation study in which they compared their results using their initial model and after the implementation of three strategies: warming up, fusing, and semi-supervised learning. In our experiments on single models (details not shown for the sake of clarity), we observed that their single initial model has a similar performance to our single model and that our model performs better in enhancing tumor region. However, the strategy that gave them the most significant improvement was the semi-supervised method. The authors used 750 additional cases from Decathlon ( [54](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8515181/#B54)) as the unlabeled data set to implement this strategy.

The best-performing method in the BraTS 2019 competition used a two-stage cascaded U-Net ( [22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8515181/#B22)). Instead of segmenting one region in each stage in their cascaded strategy, they made a coarse segmentation in the first U-Net like architecture. Then they enter the preliminary prediction map stacked with the original four input modalities into the second U-Net to make the final segmentation. The authors improved their performance implementing a multi-task learning strategy by adding a second decoder to regularize the shared encoder, using the warming up optimization method ( [57](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8515181/#B57)), performing TTA, and implementing a post-processing technique to delete false positives in the enhancing tumor region. The authors obtained similar performances using their single best model compared with fusing 12 models in an ensemble.

[Tables 3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8515181/#T3), [4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8515181/#T4) show that we got competitive results with top performance methods in the 2018 and 2019 BraTS databases, while training our models with fewer images than Isensee et al. ( [19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8515181/#B19)) and Zhao et al. ( [15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8515181/#B15)). We used less GPU memory capacity (12 GB) than Myronenko ( [21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8515181/#B21)), who trained his models on a 32 GB GPU. We obtained similar performance than cascade networks with better performance in the complete and enhancing tumor regions and with the advantage that our method segments all regions in one step. The cascade networks do it in three stages. First, the whole tumor is segmented. The tumor core is obtained using the previous segmentation to get the segmentation of the smallest region; then, the inference time is also lower in our implementation. In addition, since they used a Multi-View Fusion strategy, they need to train three networks, one for each of three different planes, to make an ensemble of the predictions; in total, nine models should be trained, three for each region. Our implementation requires training seven models.

Our qualitative results comparing top-performing methods with our proposed framework suggest that minor differences in Dice values will not always represent significant qualitative differences that could impact clinical practice.

Comparing the results obtained with the 2.5D AU-Net model in the validation and the test dataset (see [Table 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8515181/#T2)), we are confident that the proposed model generalizes well since similar general performances were obtained. Results obtained in the test set presented an increase in the values obtained in the ET region and a decrease in the WT region. This behavior is also observed in most participating models, making it possible that the dataset test images were easier to segment in the enhancing tumor region and more difficult in the whole tumor region.

Even if we did not observe overfitting behavior, we could improve the performance of our model by adding more complex data augmentation methods, such as elastic and pixel-wise transformations, since some of the top-performing methods in past editions of the BraTS challenge implemented them. However, this was not proposed as there is no clear evidence of the impact of performing more data augmentation ( [15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8515181/#B15)).

Outside the context of the BraTS challenge, there are some works on brain tumor segmentation. Most of them use hand-crafted features combined with machine learning techniques ( [45](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8515181/#B45), [58](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8515181/#B58), [59](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8515181/#B59)). Soltaninejad et al. ( [59](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8515181/#B59)) used the diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) additionally to the T1, T2, and FLAIR sequences, to improve their method, which combines super voxels and random forest models. While the reported results are comparatively lower than those reported on BraTS challenges, with a Dice value of 0.84 for the whole tumor, they propose innovative modifications that could improve the transferability of trained models.

Deep learning models like the ones trained in BraTS database can be adapted to different types of images, as illustrated by the results of another grand challenge, the Decathlon ( [54](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8515181/#B54)). In this competition, the models must be able to segment a great variety of regions of six different organs, among them the brain, the heart, and the liver, and adapt to other imaging modalities such as CT and MRI. The last winner used an ensemble of three different U-Net architectures, combining 2D and 3D implementations to fit all different image sizes and different memory consumption ( [19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8515181/#B19)). While being adaptive to many applications, the performance of this framework in the different tasks is usually lower than that of a dedicated end-to-end network.

Finally, we have explored the use of an ensemble of models to estimate structure-wise uncertainties by measuring volume variation coefficients; we observed similar behavior as observed in ( [51](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8515181/#B51)) when using test time augmentation uncertainty estimation, but we found that a quadratic relationship between segmentation error in terms of 1-Dice and structure-wise uncertainty fits better the data (see [Figure 8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8515181/#F8)) instead of a linear relationship as reported by ( [51](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8515181/#B51)).

We have compared our method using an ensemble of models to estimate voxel-wise uncertainties; with six different methods implemented by Mehta et al. ( [50](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8515181/#B50)), we found that all the other methods had a higher increase in the Dice score when filtering out uncertain voxels than our method, but this was at the expense of eliminating many true-positive and true-negative predictions. Our method was significantly superior in the final score that considers the average of the three metrics ( [Table 7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8515181/#T7)). This result suggests that our approach has a better balance between improving Dice coefficient by removing wrong predictions and not drawing too many correct predictions.

Our qualitative results in uncertainty estimation show that uncertain voxels are mainly located in the borders of the different tumor regions, which is consistent with other qualitative results in uncertainty estimation ( [50](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8515181/#B50), [60](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8515181/#B60)) and with human-rater variability. We have shown a qualitative relationship between false positives and negatives and uncertain positive and negative predictions (see [Figure 7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8515181/#F7)). Quantifying volume variations associated with uncertain positive and negative predictions would be interesting as a future direction to differentiate between possible false-positive and false-negative predictions.

Perhaps one of the most important questions is whether these algorithms have a reliable application in clinical practice. Müller et al., published that CNNs for brain tumor segmentation are not directly applicable in daily clinical practice ( [61](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8515181/#B61)). However, recent works start showing the feasibility of implementing these methods into clinical practice ( [62](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8515181/#B62), [63](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8515181/#B63)). The field continues to evolve and move toward more stable and reproducible methods for different applications such as brain tumor segmentation and stroke detection, where clinical applications are clearly on the horizon ( [64](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8515181/#B64)). Estimating uncertainties will be a crucial factor in achieving these objectives.

As a perspective work, we aim to study the use of uncertainties (both structure-wise and voxel-wise) to improve segmentation accuracy when used as a post-processing technique to filtering out uncertain predictions, taking into consideration the two groups of uncertainties (positives and negatives). Uncertainties could also be used as a reference for user interactions ( [51](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8515181/#B51)) to detect mis-segmentation. We also aim to investigate the reproducibility of this method on images coming from different databases from the clinic.

## Conclusions

We have proposed a novel end-to-end FCN architecture for pre-operative MRI tumor segmentation. We have assessed, for the first time, the use of independent input entrances into an asymmetric U-Net architecture for brain tumor segmentation. Our experimentations illustrated the benefit of the proposed 2.5D Multi-View Inception and Multi-Input module that mixes different views of the 3D images using 2.5D convolutions and the benefit of using it complementarily with a more classical 3D concatenated input in an ensemble of models. The proposed AE AU-Net segmentation aims to balance combining multiple views and different receptive fields and to maintain memory consumption low. We obtained dice scores of 0.902 ± 0.066, 0.815 ± 0.161, and 0.773 ± 0.257 for the complete, core, and enhancing tumor regions, with an overall dice of 0.83 in the BraTS 2019 validation dataset. We also applied our method in BraTS 2018 database with corresponding Dice score values of 0.908 ± 0.055, 0.838 ± 0.150, and 0.800 ± 0.230, respectively. We obtained comparative results with top-performing methods without using any additional training data and requiring less memory to train than the first place in both competitions. In addition, our approach to estimate uncertainties was comparatively superior to other six methods reported in the literature. Finally, the study of voxel-wise and structure-wise uncertainties, and their relationship with the segmentation errors, give perspectives to improve segmentation accuracy further.

Language Python \_\_notebook\_\_ linkcode ### Winning solutions of kaggle competitions: [¶](https://www.kaggleusercontent.com/kf/352267813/eyJhbGciOiJkaXIiLCJlbmMiOiJBMTI4Q0JDLUhTMjU2In0..7HbW6AuH-bJlqLwS0kSz7g.DMO33_M8Sj0dB9i5maZXj_91EC3kniEaqkTLVoTiMMF-SI-63DfDuTzZU-rzYbBEkO3eEz_hNKbzvn9FDHJqrGo6xzZAyw_CPSq-NNzypoEMAHwRd0FxwXfCOe6f1JRSS2OaNtt4TI-VzLfb74b7-hH2yv2r8XfVk2bYIh0QyzP6wb8p9Ksswj0AeXtJzeZj_jJdKCeLWQmzibGTriBJKswtUND7M4hcT1tASHeSJMU7PVI1hr0mMCcwhTS7S0cooSbTprsuCRhAYyqSlEDLIe6K46VgfhmXv7zBLLQ-biUho5gZAU4BMN4UtviPBJdW2cYVtNteEuh3MgJlyUJxYnvND65r7LucoqQYjgs0jB3y8TKWcdhosCfukqtXA25AgUHOmPScpp-prIgQGop7WdotDUVR9eT1Nx8Vc9TLQowYbZKRMQRggwc9ayPcM0YJrN6Y_YD3AR4rTlzcKeP3GNSgeRD_zIW5rgXbvADuvHiIrdJ4_3-y4PRuDpJGdRKqpMMmIbiqLG9Me83c2J1QyCoz1iWLtt4RkbV3y-oNTNdJeR89gzvb_MsLGVySPEHUZwVP_4VA_yW8KIPRxza57ChElKjal5K78po6UzN85RXHnHQTRYlbP7A-1CfzqiHJCD3d4yeI57_em0HRBPS_DA.Iu5sg7hRrI0LbhtiMaC4Tg/__results__.html?sharingControls=true\#Winning-solutions-of-kaggle-competitions:) Generally at the end of every Kaggle competition, winners and other toppers used to share their solutions in the discussion forums. But it is a tedious task to search for the competitions and then for the solutions of these competitions when we need them. I always wanted to get the links to the solutions of all past Kaggle competitions at one place. I thought it would be a very good reference point many a times. Thanks to Kaggle team for the Meta Kaggle dataset, now I am able to get them in one single place through this notebook . Thanks a lot to [@sban](https://www.kaggle.com/shivamb) for this [wonderful kernel](https://www.kaggle.com/shivamb/data-science-glossary-on-kaggle/notebook) without which I wouldn't have got this notebook. I have inlcuded only "Featured" & "Research" competitions and the competitions are ordered based on recency. The solutions are ordered based on the number of upvotes received. Have fun and Happy Kaggling.! P.S : There are few outlier discussions (which are not actually solutions) too ;) In case if you find any of the solutions missing, please post them on the comments section with links. The proposed ensemble framework, combining VGG16, Xception, ResNet50, and DenseNet201, further improved performance, achieving a AUC of 0.987.

The overall accuracy increases from 94.21% to 97.38%, while the mean AUC rises from 0.965 to 0.987, indicating enhanced discriminative capability and generalization.

A deep transfer learning and ensemble learning framework for brain tumor detection and classification in MRI images


[Download PDF](https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y.pdf)

## Abstract

This study proposes a novel framework that integrates Transfer Learning (TL) and Ensemble Learning (EL) for multi-class classification of brain tumors using Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) images. The classification targets four categories: glioma, meningioma, pituitary tumor, and no tumor. Several state-of-the-art deep learning architectures from the VGG, Inception, ResNet, and DenseNet families were analyzed and compared. Based on their performance, six Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs)—VGG16, VGG19, InceptionV3, Xception, ResNet152, and DenseNet201—were selected for transfer learning to perform the classification task. To enhance classification accuracy, ensemble learning was applied using a weighted voting strategy, where the accuracy of each model served as its weight. The four top-performing models VGG16, Xception, ResNet152, and DenseNet201 were combined in this ensemble. To further interpret the model’s decisions, Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) technique, specifically Grad-CAM, was employed to highlight key regions in the MRI images that influenced the classification outcomes, thereby improving model transparency. The models were trained and evaluated on the publicly available BT-7023 dataset from Kaggle, consisting of 7,023 MRI images (5,712 for training and 1,311 for testing). Performance was assessed using accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. The proposed ensemble method achieved excellent results, with 99.28% accuracy, 98.62% precision, 99.56% recall, and a 98.58% F1-score. To verify the robustness of the approach, cross-dataset validation was conducted using an external dataset from Figshare. The proposed ensemble outperformed existing models on this dataset, achieving 98.80% accuracy. Overall, the ensemble framework demonstrated a 5%–13% performance improvement over existing methods, underscoring its effectiveness and reliability for early detection and classification of brain tumors. Additionally, the XAI-based analysis confirmed the model’s focus on clinically relevant tumor regions, enhancing interpretability and trustworthiness in medical applications.

## 1 Introduction

Brain tumors result from abnormal and uncontrolled cell growth in different brain regions, leading to severe neurological impairments and reduced quality of life \[ [1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#ref-CR1 "Celik M, Inik O. Development of hybrid models based on deep learning and optimized machine learning algorithms for brain tumor multi-classification. Expert Syst Appl. 2024;238:122159.")\]. Owing to their clinical severity and diagnostic complexity, they remain a major medical challenge \[ [2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#ref-CR2 "Sharif M, Amin J, Raza M, Yasmin M, Satapathy SC. An integrated design of particle swarm optimization (pso) with fusion of features for detection of brain tumor. Pattern Recogn Lett. 2020;129:150–7.")\]. Brain tumors commonly include glioma (GL), meningioma (ME), pituitary (PT), and no-tumor (NT) cases, with gliomas, meningiomas, and pituitary tumors being the most prevalent primary brain tumors \[ [3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#ref-CR3 "Ahmed MM, Hossain MM, Islam MR, et al. Brain tumor detection and classification in MRI using hybrid ViT and GRU model with explainable AI in Southern Bangladesh. Sci Rep. 2024;14:22797.                    https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-024-71893-3                                    ."), [4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#ref-CR4 "Nodirov J, Abdusalomov AB, Whangbo TK. Attention 3D U-Net with Multiple Skip Connections for Segmentation of Brain Tumor Images. Sensors. 2022;22:6501.")\]. Meningiomas typically originate from the meninges surrounding the brain and spinal cord and are generally benign \[ [5](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#ref-CR5 "Shafi ASM, Rahman MB, Anwar T, Halder RS, Kays HE. Classification of brain tumors and auto-immune disease using ensemble learning. Inf Med Unlocked. 2021;24:100608.")\], whereas gliomas arise from glial cells, account for nearly one-third of brain tumor cases, and exhibit the highest mortality rates \[ [6](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#ref-CR6 "Pereira S, Pinto A, Alves V, Silva CA. Brain tumor segmentation using convolutional neural networks in MRI images. IEEE Trans Med Imaging. 2016;35:1240–51.")\]. Pituitary tumors develop within the pituitary gland and are usually less aggressive \[ [7](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#ref-CR7 "Ahuja S, Panigrahi BK, Gandhi TK. Enhanced performance of Dark-Nets for brain tumor classification and segmentation using colormap-based superpixel techniques. Mach Learn Appl. 2022;7:100212.")\].

Brain tumors can cause significant physical and neurological impairments, often necessitating intensive treatment. The severity of symptoms depends on tumor type, size, and location. Accurate tumor classification using MRI is critical for diagnosis, treatment planning, and improved patient outcomes. Early detection enhances survival rates and quality of life; however, manual image interpretation is time-consuming and prone to human error \[ [8](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#ref-CR8 "Lan Y-L, Zou S, Qin B, Zhu X. Potential roles of transformers in brain tumor diagnosis and treatment. Brain-X. 2023;1:e23."), [9](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#ref-CR9 "Ranjbarzadeh R, Zarbakhsh P, Caputo A, Tirkolaee EB, Bendechache M. Brain tumor segmentation based on optimized convolutional neural network and improved chimp optimization algorithm. Comput Biol Med. 2024;168:107723.")\]. Medical imaging, particularly MRI, plays a central role in brain tumor diagnosis due to its high spatial resolution and non-invasive nature \[ [10](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#ref-CR10 "Mudda M, Manjunath R, Krishnamurthy N. Brain tumor classification using enhanced statistical texture features. IETE J Res. 2022;68:3695–706."), [11](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#ref-CR11 "Sajid S, Hussain S, Sarwar A. Brain tumor detection and segmentation in MR images using deep learning. Arab J Sci Eng. 2019;44:9249–61.")\].

Despite technological advances, the diagnostic process \[ [128](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#ref-CR128 "Tian J, Luo H, Wu S, Yan P, Zhang J. Source-free domain adaptation for open-set cross-domain fault diagnosis. IEEE Trans Industr Inf. 2025;21(12):9341–52.                    https://doi.org/10.1109/TII.2025.3598445                                    .")\] remains complex and heavily reliant on radiologist expertise. Increasing imaging volumes and inter-patient variability in tumor characteristics reduce efficiency and increase diagnostic cost \[ [8](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#ref-CR8 "Lan Y-L, Zou S, Qin B, Zhu X. Potential roles of transformers in brain tumor diagnosis and treatment. Brain-X. 2023;1:e23.")\]. Automated classification systems address these challenges by enabling objective, reproducible, and efficient image analysis, thereby improving diagnostic reliability \[ [12](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#ref-CR12 "Castiglioni I, et al. Ai applications to medical images: From machine learning to deep learning. Phys Med. 2021;83:9–24."), [129](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#ref-CR129 "Tian J, Luo H, Wu S, et al. A transfer gated recurrent unit model for battery health monitoring under cross-domain conditions. IEEE Trans Instrum Meas. 2025;74(1–12).                    https://doi.org/10.1109/TIM.2025.3548227                                    . Art. 3516612.")\].

The rapid development of Artificial Intelligence (AI), especially Deep Learning (DL), has significantly advanced medical image analysis \[ [13](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#ref-CR13 "Arabahmadi M, Farahbakhsh R, Rezazadeh J. Deep Learning for Smart Healthcare—A Survey on Brain Tumor Detection from Medical Imaging, Sensors, no. 5, p. 1960, Mar. 2022.                    https://doi.org/10.3390/s22051960                                    ")\]. DL-based methods, particularly convolutional neural networks (CNNs), demonstrate strong capability in learning complex patterns from large datasets, making them highly effective for brain tumor classification \[ [14](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#ref-CR14 "Gurusamy R, Subramaniam V. A machine learning approach for MRI brain tumor classification. Comput Mater Continua. 2017;53:91–109."), [15](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#ref-CR15 "Md AA, Sheikh T, Maity. Alok Kole IRU-Net: An Efficient End-to-End Network for Automatic Building Extraction from Remote Sensing Images. IEEE Access. 2022;10:37811–28.                    https://doi.org/10.1109/ACCESS.2022.3164401                                    .")\]. AI-assisted diagnosis has improved neuropathological confidence and clinical decision-making \[ [16](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#ref-CR16 "Hollon TC, Pandian B, Adapa AR, Urias E, Save AV, Khalsa SSS, Eichberg DG, D’Amico RS, Farooq ZU, Lewis S, et al. Near real-time intraoperative brain tumor diagnosis using stimulated Raman histology and deep neural networks. Nat Med. 2020;26:52–8."), [17](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#ref-CR17 "Ali MS, Hossain MM, Kona MA, Nowrin KR, Islam MK. An ensemble classification approach for cervical cancer prediction using behavioral risk factors. Healthc Anal. 2024;5:100324.")\].

Nevertheless, challenges such as dataset imbalance, high computational requirements, and tumor heterogeneity persist. Numerous Machine Learning (ML) and DL approaches have been explored, including SVM, k-NN, decision trees, Random Forest, Naive Bayes \[ [14](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#ref-CR14 "Gurusamy R, Subramaniam V. A machine learning approach for MRI brain tumor classification. Comput Mater Continua. 2017;53:91–109."), [42](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#ref-CR42 "Amin J, Sharif M, Haldorai A, Yasmin M, Nayak RS. Brain tumor detection and classification using machine learning: A comprehensive survey. Complex Intell Syst. 2022;8:3161–83.")\], and DL architectures such as CNNs, VGGNet \[ [18](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#ref-CR18 "Simonyan K, Zisserman A. Very deep convolutional networks for large-scale image recognition. arXiv. 2014. arXiv:1409.1556.")\], GoogleNet \[ [19](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#ref-CR19 "Szegedy C, Liu W, Jia Y, Sermanet P, Reed S, Anguelov D, Erhan D, Vanhoucke V, Rabinovich A. Going deeper with convolutions. In Proceedings of the 2015 IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern RecognitionWorkshops (CVPRW), Boston, MA, USA, 7–12 June 2015; pp. 1–9.")\], ResNet \[ [20](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#ref-CR20 "He K, Zhang X, Ren S, Sun J. Deep residual learning for image recognition. In Proceedings of the 2016 IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR), Las Vegas, NV, USA, 27–30 June 2016; pp. 770–778.")\], MobileNet, Inception, and DenseNet \[ [21](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#ref-CR21 "Khaliki MZ, Başarslan MS. Brain tumor detection from images and comparison with transfer learning methods and 3-layer CNN. Sci Rep. 2024;14:1–10."), [22](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#ref-CR22 "Fathima N, Kumar P. This work proposes a deployment-aware heterogeneous ensemble of transfer-learned CNNs that jointly improves classification accuracy, cross-dataset generalization, and interpretability for brain tumor MRI analysis. Unlike existing ensemble or single-model transfer-learning approaches, the proposed method leverages heterogeneous pretrained CNNs, systematic ablation, cross-dataset validation, and interpretability analysis to jointly address accuracy, robustness, and clinical deployability. Unlike prior works that rely on single CNN architectures or unweighted ensembles, our method integrates (i) the unified integration of transfer learning, ensemble learning and explainable AI within a single pipeline, (ii) performance-guided weighted voting, (iii) cross-dataset evaluation to demonstrate generalization.

The proposed framework effectively addresses key challenges such as data imbalance, limited interpretability, and variability in imaging. By incorporating XAI and leveraging diverse data sources, the model demonstrates improved generalizability across different populations and imaging conditions, making it a more adaptable and clinically relevant solution for brain tumor diagnosis.

As illustrated in the workflow, the proposed framework consists of five key stages:

1. (a)
Preprocessing and Data Augmentation: MRI brain tumor images undergo several preprocessing steps to standardize the dataset for classification tasks. Images from the Kaggle and Figshare datasets are split into training and testing sets in an 80:20 ratio. To address class imbalance between tumor and no-tumor categories, data augmentation techniques—such as rotation, zooming, and flipping—are applied to increase the diversity and quantity of training samples for each class.

2. (b)
Transfer Learning: A set of pre-trained CNNs, including VGG16, VGG19, InceptionV3, Xception, ResNet152 and DenseNet201, are fine-tuned using TL to adapt to the brain tumor classification task. Based on performance metrics, the top four models are selected to serve as base classifiers for the ensemble stage.

3. (c)
Ensemble Learning: To further enhance classification accuracy, a weighted voting ensemble method is employed. In this approach, the classification accuracy of each selected model is used as its voting weight, allowing the ensemble to benefit from the strengths of the most accurate models.

4. (d)
Evaluation: The model’s performance is assessed using standard classification metrics, including accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score and AUC, to comprehensively evaluate its effectiveness across all tumor categories.

5. (e)
Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI): To improve transparency and interpretability, the Grad-CAM visualization technique is utilized. This XAI method highlights the critical regions in MRI images that influence the model’s predictions, offering insights into its decision-making process and supporting clinical trust in automated diagnosis.


The key contributions of this study are outlined as follows:

1. (a)
Unlike existing ensemble approaches that typically combine homogeneous models or apply simple majority/soft voting without analyzing complementary representations, the proposed method employs a heterogeneous ensemble of transfer-learned CNN backbones, explicitly designed to capture diverse spatial and semantic features. This heterogeneity-driven integration is the key innovation that differentiates the method from conventional ensemble strategies.

2. (b)
In contrast to most TL-based studies that fine-tune a single pretrained network, the proposed framework performs a systematic multi-backbone transfer learning analysis followed by ensemble integration. This enables a direct assessment of individual TL models versus their ensemble, clearly demonstrating that the performance gain arises from the proposed integration strategy rather than isolated model selection.

3. (c)
Existing Ensemble and TL work primarily emphasize accuracy on a single dataset. The proposed method extends beyond this by incorporating cross-dataset validation, ensemble-level Grad-CAM interpretability, and computational/deployment analysis, thereby addressing robustness, transparency, and real-world feasibility—dimensions that are largely unexplored in prior Ensemble/TL approaches.

4. (d)
The key contributions of this work are summarized into three core innovations:


- The unified integration of transfer learning, ensemble learning, and explainable AI within a single pipeline,

- A weighted ensemble of deep transfer learning models optimized via validation accuracy;

- Robust evaluation through cross-dataset validation and augmentation ablation;

- Clinically interpretable decision support using Grad-CAM visual explanations.


The rest of the paper is organized as follows: Sect.  2 reviews recent DL approaches for brain tumor detection. Section  [3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#Sec9) details the proposed classification framework based on TL and ML with XAI tools such as Grad-CAM. Section  4 discusses the experimental setup and results. Finally, Sect.  5 concludes the paper and suggests future research directions.

Variation in preprocessing steps e.g., resizing, normalization, augmentation across studies complicates comparisons and reproducibility. There is strong need for DL models to implement advanced preprocessing, but standardized pipelines.

Recent advancements in deep learning for medical image analysis have extended beyond traditional convolutional and transformer-based approaches to encompass multimodal and model-compression paradigms. Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have emerged as a prominent class of multimodal deep learning frameworks that integrate visual and textual information, enabling more effective semantic understanding across tasks such as classification, segmentation, report generation, and visual question answering in medical imaging \[ [125](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#ref-CR125 "Li X, Li L, Jiang Y, Wang H, Qiao X, Feng T, Luo H, Zhao Y. Vision-language models in medical image analysis: From simple fusion to general large models. Inform Fusion. 2025;118:102995.                    https://doi.org/10.1016/j.inffus.2025.102995                                    .")\]. These models evolve from early simple fusion strategies to more general large model formulations that leverage pre-training and fine-tuning to enhance cross-modal interactions and downstream performance, addressing challenges like limited annotated data and enhancing interpretability through textual alignment with visual features. For instance, recent surveys highlight how VLM architectures, through contrastive and attention-based fusion mechanisms, improve representation learning and facilitate complex clinical tasks by jointly modeling image and language semantics \[ [126](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#ref-CR126 "Ryu JS, Kang H, Chu Y, et al. Vision-language foundation models for medical imaging: A review of current practices and innovations. Biomed Eng Lett. 2025;15:809–30.                    https://doi.org/10.1007/s13534-025-00484-6                                    .")\].

Alongside multimodal modeling, knowledge distillation (KD) and teacher-student learning frameworks have gained significant traction in medical imaging research as effective means to transfer expertise from high-capacity models to lightweight counterparts \[ [127](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#ref-CR127 "Li X, Li L, Li M, Yan P, Feng T, Luo H, Zhao Y, Yin S. Knowledge distillation and teacher–student learning in medical imaging: Comprehensive overview, pivotal role, and future directions. Medical Image Analysis 107(Pt A). 2026;103819.                    https://doi.org/10.1016/j.media.2025.103819                                    .")\]. KD techniques have been applied across diverse tasks such as classification, segmentation, detection, and reconstruction, where distilled models retain competitive performance with reduced computational overhead, expanding clinical deployability and addressing annotation scarcity. These developments underscore the growing trend of incorporating large foundation models and efficient model adaptation strategies in medical image analysis, highlighting future directions toward generalizable, scalable, and clinically robust AI systems.

Overall, earlier models for brain tumor detection faced challenges such as low accuracy, class imbalance, high computational demands, and limited interpretability. The proposed ensemble-based model in this research addresses these issues, offering improved accuracy, better handling of data imbalance, and enhanced interpretability. Its adaptability across various datasets and imaging sources underscores its potential for broad clinical application.

## 3 Proposed methodology

The workflow of the proposed model, illustrated in Fig. [1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#Fig1), employs six widely recognized transfer learning architectures—VGG16, VGG19, InceptionV3, Xception, ResNet152, and DenseNet201—for classifying brain tumors in MRI images into four categories: glioma, meningioma, pituitary tumor, and no tumor. To enhance classification performance, an ensemble learning approach based on a weighted voting strategy is adopted. Among the six models, the four best-performing CNN architectures—VGG16, Xception, ResNet152, and DenseNet201 are selected for the ensemble. Furthermore, to improve the transparency and interpretability of the model’s predictions, XAI techniques are applied. Specifically, Grad-CAM \[ [74](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#ref-CR74 "Khan MA, Hussain MZ, Mehmood S, Khan MF, Ahmad M, Mazhar T, Shahzad T, Saeed MM. Transfer learning for accurate brain tumor classification in MRI: a step forward in medical diagnostics. Discov Oncol. 2025;16(1):1040.                    https://doi.org/10.1007/s12672-025-02671-4                                    . PMID: 40490586; PMCID: PMC12149374.")\] is used to generate visual explanations by highlighting critical regions in the MRI scans that contribute to the model’s decision-making process.

### 3.1 Transfer learning model evaluation

Transfer learning (TL) adapts pre-trained models to new tasks \[ [27](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#ref-CR27 "Mathivanan SK, Sonaimuthu S, Murugesan S, et al. Employing deep learning and transfer learning for accurate brain tumor detection. Sci Rep. 2024;14:7232.                    https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-024-57970-7                                    .")\] and is particularly beneficial in medical imaging scenarios with limited labeled data, offering a resource-efficient alternative to training models from scratch. TL significantly reduces development time for high-performing models in complex tasks such as image recognition and natural language processing \[ [91](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#ref-CR91 "Zheng Y, Li C, Zhou X, Chen H, Xu H, Li Y, Zhang H, Li X, Sun H, Huang X, Grzegorzek M. Application of transfer learning and ensemble learning in image-level classification for breast histopathology. Intell Med. 2023;3(2):115–28.                    https://doi.org/10.1016/j.imed.2022.05.004                                    .")\].

This study investigates deep transfer learning architectures to improve brain tumor classification accuracy. Four CNN families—VGG, Inception, ResNet, and DenseNet—were evaluated using RGB images resized to 224 × 224 pixels. Six pre-trained models (VGG16, VGG19, InceptionV3, Xception, ResNet152, and DenseNet201) were selected due to their robustness, high accuracy, and complementary feature-learning capabilities.

All six CNNs were pre-trained on the ImageNet dataset prior to task-specific fine-tuning. Next, the front-end layers of the trained models in these six CNNs are frozen to preserve the learned features and prevent any loss of information during subsequent training. Subsequently, the augmented brain Tumor images and their corresponding labels are used to fine-tune the fully connected layers at the back ends of the six networks. This allows the classification knowledge gained from ImageNet to be effectively transferred to the target test data. The following sub-sections provide a brief overview of the CNN models employed for TL in this study.

#### 3.1.1 Visual geometry group 16

VGGNet ranked among the top two performers in the 2014 ImageNet Large-Scale Visual Recognition Challenge (ILSVRC) \[ [18](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#ref-CR18 "Simonyan K, Zisserman A. Very deep convolutional networks for large-scale image recognition. arXiv. 2014. arXiv:1409.1556."), [92](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#ref-CR92 "Russakovsky O, Deng J, Su H, et al. Very deep convolutional networks for large-scale image recognition. arXiv. 2014. arXiv:1409.1556.")\], the VGG16 model is a widely used variant within the VGG network family. Similar to AlexNet \[ [18](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#ref-CR18 "Simonyan K, Zisserman A. Very deep convolutional networks for large-scale image recognition. arXiv. 2014. arXiv:1409.1556."), [95](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#ref-CR95 "Bansa M, Kumar M, Sachdeva M, Mittal A. Transfer learning and SE-ResNet152 networks-based for small-scale unbalanced fish species identification. Comput Electron Agric. 2023;180(1):1–7.")\], VGG16 is a deep CNN designed for image classification and object detection. One of its key strengths lies in its ability to effectively manage large-scale datasets and handle complex visual recognition tasks \[ [93](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#ref-CR93 "Liu M, Yi M, Wu M, Wang J, He Y. #### 3.1.3 ResNet152

ResNet-152, designed by Microsoft Research, is a deep convolutional neural network consisting of 152 layers \[ [96](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#ref-CR96 "Xu X, Li W, Duan Q. Transfer learning and SE-ResNet152 networks-based for small-scale unbalanced fish species identification. Comput Electron Agric. 2023;180(1):1–7.")\]. Its standout feature is the use of residual or skip connections, which allow the model to learn residual functions, significantly simplifying the training of very deep networks \[ [96](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#ref-CR96 "Xu X, Li W, Duan Q. Transfer learning and SE-ResNet152 networks-based for small-scale unbalanced fish species identification. Comput Electron Agric. 2023;180(1):1–7.")\]. The considerable depth of ResNet-152 enables it to capture complex features and patterns within data, making it highly effective for tasks such as image classification and object recognition. Combined with residual connections, this deep architecture overcomes the vanishing gradient problem, allowing efficient training of very deep networks. The Xception network is an enhanced variant of InceptionV3 and is often considered an “extreme” version of the Inception architecture \[ [102](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#ref-CR102 "Chollet F. Xception: deep learning with depth wise separable convolutions. In: Pro-ceedings of the IEEE conference on computer vision and pattern recognition; 2017. pp. 1251–8.")\]. It incorporates depthwise separable convolutions, achieving strong performance when applied to extensive training datasets. In contrast, ResNet is built on fundamental modules called residual blocks, which effectively address the issue of vanishing gradients in deep neural networks \[ [103](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#ref-CR103 "He K, Zhang X, Ren S et al. Proceedings of the IEEE conference on computer vision and pattern recognition; 2016. pp. 770–8.")\]. #### 3.1.6 DenseNet201

DenseNet201 is a deep convolutional neural network designed to alleviate the vanishing gradient problem, enhance feature propagation and feature utilization, and reduce the overall number of network parameters \[ [101](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#ref-CR101 "Huang G, Liu Z, Van Der Maaten L, Weinberger KQ. (2017) Densely Connected Convolutional Networks. Proceedings of the IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition, Honolulu, 21–26 July 2017, 4700–4708.                    https://doi.org/10.1109/CVPR.2017.243                                    ")\]. The DenseNet201 architecture establishes direct connections between all layers, enabling comprehensive information flow throughout the network \[ [101](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#ref-CR101 "Huang G, Liu Z, Van Der Maaten L, Weinberger KQ. (2017) Densely Connected Convolutional Networks. Proceedings of the IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition, Honolulu, 21–26 July 2017, 4700–4708.                    https://doi.org/10.1109/CVPR.2017.243                                    ")\]. During forward propagation, each layer is directly connected to all preceding layers, receiving their outputs as its input. Compared to traditional convolutional neural networks like ResNet, which primarily rely on the features output from the final layers, DenseNet201 is able to fuse and leverage a greater number of low-level features. This leads to improved efficiency in both feature propagation and utilization. The DenseNet201 architecture is primarily composed of dense blocks and transition layers, as illustrated in Fig. [7](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#Fig7).

### 4.2 Data preprocessing and augmentation

To standardize the input data for brain tumor classification, a series of preprocessing steps were applied. All MRI images were resized to 224 × 224 pixels to ensure uniformity across all models. RGB images were converted to grayscale, followed by Gaussian blur filtering to reduce noise and enhance image quality while preserving essential features. High-pass filtering was then used to sharpen the images and emphasize fine details. These preprocessed images, along with their corresponding labels, served as input for model training and evaluation.

To address limited data availability and improve generalization, data augmentation was performed using Keras’ _ImageDataGenerator_. Techniques such as rotation, zoom, flipping, and shifting were applied to synthetically expand the dataset and simulate variability in real-world medical imaging. This not only enhanced model robustness and reduced overfitting but also balanced class distributions \[ [106](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#ref-CR106 "Zhang C, Bengio S, Hardt M, Recht B, Vinyals O. Understanding deep learning (still) requires rethinking generalization. Commun ACM. 2021;64:107–15."), [107](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#ref-CR107 "Buslaev A, Iglovikov VI, Khvedchenya E, Parinov A, Druzhinin M, Kalinin AA, Albumentations. Fast and flexible image augmentations. Information. 2020;11:125.")\]. This augmentation-based strategy has proven effective in improving the overall performance of deep learning models, resulting in higher accuracy \[ [106](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#ref-CR106 "Zhang C, Bengio S, Hardt M, Recht B, Vinyals O. Understanding deep learning (still) requires rethinking generalization. Commun ACM. 2021;64:107–15."), [107](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#ref-CR107 "Buslaev A, Iglovikov VI, Khvedchenya E, Parinov A, Druzhinin M, Kalinin AA, Albumentations. Fast and flexible image augmentations. Information. 2020;11:125.")\]. In total, data augmentation increased the training dataset from 10,087 to 35,583 images. Data augmentation was applied exclusively to the training set. No augmented samples were used in validation or testing, thereby fully preventing data leakage. In particular, we have applied augmentation before dataset splitting can lead to data leakage, where augmented variants of the same image may appear across training and testing sets, resulting in overly optimistic performance estimates. To mitigate this risk, dataset splitting was performed prior to augmentation, and all augmented samples were derived solely from the original training images. Additionally, all images were normalized to ensure consistent pixel value distribution. Figure [10](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#Fig10) illustrates examples of original and augmented MRI images, and Table [3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#Tab3) summarizes the dataset composition.

### 4.5 Evaluation metrics

The performance of the proposed transfer learning models is assessed using a confusion matrix, which enables the calculation of key evaluation metrics such as precision, recall (sensitivity), F1-score, AUC and accuracy \[ [15](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#ref-CR15 "Md AA, Sheikh T, Maity. IEEE Access. 2022;10:37811–28.                    https://doi.org/10.1109/ACCESS.2022.3164401                                    .")\]. Structured as an _n × n_ square matrix for _n_-class classification problems, the confusion matrix provides a comprehensive view of the model’s prediction outcomes \[ [91](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#ref-CR91 "Zheng Y, Li C, Zhou X, Chen H, Xu H, Li Y, Zhang H, Li X, Sun H, Huang X, Grzegorzek M. Specifically, TP refers to tumor cases correctly identified by the model, FP denotes non-tumor cases wrongly classified as tumors, FN accounts for tumor cases missed by the model, and TN indicates non-tumor cases correctly predicted. The F1-score, defined as the harmonic mean of precision and recall.

### 4.6 Valuation of results and analysis of model performance

We carried out a thorough evaluation of our model’s performance through the examination of various performance metrics. In this study, six state-of-the-art CNN architectures—VGG16, VGG19, ResNet152, InceptionV3, Xception, and DenseNet201 were employed for TL to identify the most effective networks and four optimized ensemble deep learning models are used for accurate brain tumor classification. To provide a comparative analysis, the same six CNN models were also trained from scratch. Table [4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#Tab4) outlines the training parameters for each model. For training the network from scratch, the input size was set to 224 × 224 × 3, with the batch sizes for the VGG16, VGG19, InceptionV3, Xception, ResNet152, and DenseNet201 networks were set to 32, 16, 26, 8, 26 and 16, respectively. The epoch was specified as 40. For transfer learning, the input size was increased to 460 × 460 × 3, the batch size was fixed at 16, and the number of epochs remained at 40. The classification outcomes of the six CNN models, using both training approaches, are summarized in Table [6](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#Tab6). The statistical results presented in the table demonstrate that TL generally outperformed training models from scratch, yielding an improvement in accuracy ranging from approximately 3% to 13%, a notably positive result. Interestingly, the InceptionV3 network was an exception; when trained from scratch, it achieved slightly better performance than its transfer learning counterpart, with an accuracy higher by 0.62%. Additionally, its recall and F1-score were also superior in the scratch-trained version, registering values of 99.18% and 94.85%, respectively. Despite these results, transfer learning with InceptionV3 was still selected for further experiments. This decision was driven primarily by the significantly longer training time required when starting from scratch exceeding two hours under the given computational setup. As a result, transfer learning was adopted across all models for the subsequent stages of experimentation.

### 4.8 Ensemble learning

Ensemble learning is a powerful machine learning paradigm where multiple models are combined to solve a particular problem e.g., classification, regression with better accuracy, robustness, and generalization than any single model \[ [28](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#ref-CR28 "Thompson S, Anderson J, Roberts E. Brain tumor detection using deep learning with an ensemble of convolutional neural networks. J Med Imaging. 2022;12(3):145–58.")\]. Ensemble pruning is a technique used in ensemble learning to select a subset of trained individual learners rather than utilizing the all-ensemble learners \[ [91](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#ref-CR91 "Zheng Y, Li C, Zhou X, Chen H, Xu H, Li Y, Zhang H, Li X, Sun H, Huang X, Grzegorzek M. Application of transfer learning and ensemble learning in image-level classification for breast histopathology. Intell Med. 2023;3(2):115–28.                    https://doi.org/10.1016/j.imed.2022.05.004                                    .")\]. This approach offers two key advantages. First, it enables ensemble predictions with a reduced network scale, which lowers both storage requirements and computational costs associated with processing each learner’s output, thereby enhancing overall model efficiency. Second, by eliminating redundant or less effective models, ensemble pruning can improve the generalization performance compared to using all available learners.

In this study, two classifiers with comparatively lower performance were pruned from the six TL-based CNN models. The remaining four VGG16, Xception, ResNet152, and DenseNet201 were selected as the final individual learners for further analysis. Since classification accuracy was the primary evaluation criterion, each model’s _accuracy_ was used as a weight in the ensemble’s voting mechanism. In this method, first, each weight is quantized using a step size of 0.01, forming a discrete set \\(\\{0,0.01,0.02,...,0.99,1\\}\\). Then, for weight vector \\({w}\_{k=1,2,\\dots,6}\\), the combination of \\({w}\_{(k,1)},{w}\_{(k,2)}\\), and \\({w}\_{(k,3)}\\) leading to the highest matching \\({accuracy}\_{k}\\) is selected. Finally, the selected weights \\({w}\_{k=1,2,\\dots,6}\\)are implemented in the ensemble learning process. In this way, we found an ensemble accuracy of 99.28%.

In summary, the final model was developed through the following steps. First, to address data imbalance, the Kaggle dataset was augmented using rotations, zooming, horizontal and vertical flipping techniques. The augmented dataset was then used to train six individual CNN classifiers based on transfer learning. Next, the four best-performing classifiers were selected and combined using a weighted voting ensemble strategy. Finally, the performance of the ensemble model was evaluated.

### 4.9 Evaluation of ensemble learning algorithms

After training, the system’s overall performance was evaluated using four key metrics: accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. The confusion matrix for the ensemble model, presented in Fig. [14](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#Fig14), illustrates its classification results on the unseen test dataset. The ensemble model correctly identified 387 images as glioma, 345 as no tumor, 338 as meningioma, and 320 as pituitary tumor. However, it misclassified a few instances: three tumor cases were entirely missed; one pituitary tumor was misclassified as meningioma; three pituitary tumors were labeled as glioma; two glioma cases were mistaken for meningioma; one glioma image was classified as pituitary; and five meningioma samples were predicted as glioma.

Among the four classes, meningioma exhibited the highest False Negative Rate (FNR), which contributed to its comparatively lower accuracy, as evident from the confusion matrix. In contrast, pituitary tumors achieved the highest classification performance across all four metrics. As shown in Table [7](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#Tab7), pituitary tumors attained a recall of 98.461%, precision of 99.071%, F1-score of 98.473%, and overall accuracy of 99.427%. Glioma, known to be one of the most malignant and prevalent brain tumors, was classified with a recall of 99.231% and an accuracy of 98.144%, demonstrating the model’s strong performance in identifying this critical class. Similarly, the ensemble approach showed robust performance for the other classes as well, with correct classification rates of 99.144% for meningioma and 99.427% for no tumor cases. Among the three tumor types, pituitary tumors had the highest detection and precision rates, while meningioma had the lowest detection rate. The ensemble model demonstrated consistent performance, achieving an overall training accuracy of 98.856% and testing accuracy of 97.845%.

The consistent upward shift of the ensemble ROC curve toward the top-left corner reflects improved true positive rates at lower false positive rates, demonstrating that integrating complementary feature representations from multiple deep networks significantly enhances model robustness and generalization for multi-class brain tumor classification.

These results confirm that the proposed framework provides reliable threshold-independent performance and complements the conventional evaluation metrics such as accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. The inclusion of ROC–AUC analysis further validates the robustness and generalization capability of the model for clinical brain tumor diagnosis.

### 4.10 Model efficiency

To address the model efficiency, we further compared the computational cost of different models in terms of floating-point of operations (FLOPs), the number of trainable parameters \[ [87](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#ref-CR87 "Rai HM, Chatterjee K. ‘‘2D MRI image analysis and brain tumor detection using deep learning CNN model LeU-Net,’’ Multimedia Tools Appl., vol. 80, nos. 28–29, pp. 36111–36141, Nov. 2021,                    https://doi.org/10.1007/s11042-021-11504-9                                    ")\] and memory size. The amount of computation consumption of all models is calculated on a 256 × 256 image. Table [10](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#Tab10) presents the computational complexity and memory requirements of all evaluated architectures. VGG16 and VGG19 exhibit the highest parameter counts, with 138.4 M and 143.7 M parameters, respectively, resulting in substantial memory footprints of 528 MB and 549 MB and FLOPs of 15.5 G and 19.6 G per inference. In contrast, InceptionV3 and Xception are considerably more efficient, requiring only 23.8 M and 22.9 M parameters, with FLOPs of 5.7 G and 8.4 G and memory usage below 100 MB. ResNet152 shows moderate complexity with 60.2 M parameters, 11.3 G FLOPs, and 230 MB memory, while DenseNet201 is the most lightweight backbone, using 20.0 M parameters, 4.3 G FLOPs, and 77 MB memory. The proposed ensemble model, formed by integrating multiple deep backbones, achieves the highest representational capacity with 265.3 M parameters, 21.6 G FLOPs, and a memory footprint of 1015 MB. Although computationally more demanding, this ensemble delivers superior diagnostic performance, and its deployment can be facilitated through standard optimization techniques such as quantization, pruning, and knowledge distillation to meet real-time clinical requirements.

### 4.12 Grad-CAM explainable artificial intelligence

Explainable AI (XAI) \[ [29](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#ref-CR29 "Iftikhar S, Anjum N, Siddiqui AB, et al. Explainable CNN for brain tumor detection and classification through XAI based key features identification. Brain Inf. 2025;12:10.                    https://doi.org/10.1186/s40708-025-00257-y                                    .")\] is essential for transparency in AI systems, especially in healthcare where model decisions directly affect patient outcomes \[ [108](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#ref-CR108 "Hossain MM, et al. cardiovascular disease identification using a hybrid cnn-lstm model with explainable AI. Inf Med Unlocked. 2023;42:101370.")\]. In brain tumor classification, methods like CAM, Grad-CAM, LIME, SHAP, and Attention Maps improve deep learning model interpretability \[ [31](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#ref-CR31 "Mahim S, et al. Unlocking the potential of XAI for improved alzheimer’s disease detection and classification using a ViT-GRU model. IEEE Access. 2024;12:8390–412.")\]. We incorporated XAI into our proposed model to provide insight into its decision-making process and enhance clinical trust. Specifically, Grad-CAM \[ [30](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#ref-CR30 "Selvaraju RR, Cogswell M, Das A, Vedantam R, Parikh D, Batra D. Grad-cam: Visual explanations from deep networks via gradient-based localization, in Proceedings of the IEEE International Conference on Computer Vision. 2017; 618–626.")\] was employed for its strong spatial localization, enabling clear visualization of tumor regions in MRI scans.

Grad-CAM \[ [30](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#ref-CR30 "Selvaraju RR, Cogswell M, Das A, Vedantam R, Parikh D, Batra D. Grad-cam: Visual explanations from deep networks via gradient-based localization, in Proceedings of the IEEE International Conference on Computer Vision. 2017; 618–626.")\], an extension of CAM, is a widely used XAI technique for visualizing CNN decision processes. It generates class-specific heatmaps by computing the gradients of the predicted class with respect to the final convolutional layer’s activations, thereby highlighting the most influential regions in MRI images for brain tumor classification. In our XAI-integrated CNN architecture, Grad-CAM was applied by performing a forward pass to obtain predictions, followed by a backward pass to compute importance weights from the gradients. These weights were used to create activation maps, emphasizing regions critical to the model’s decision. ReLU was applied to retain only positive contributions, and the resulting maps were overlaid on the original images, offering interpretable visualizations of model focus across different layers.

### 4.13 Explainability results

By employing XAI techniques such as Grad-CAM, we enhanced the interpretability of our model, highlighting critical regions that assist clinicians in understanding its decisions. The collaborating radiologist validated the model’s outputs and provided positive feedback on its decision-making, facilitated by the integration of XAI. This interpretability fosters trust, ensuring the model’s reliability and alignment with clinical reasoning, thereby strengthening its applicability in real-world healthcare settings. Our findings, illustrated through multiple figures, demonstrate the model’s ability to accurately capture brain tumor pathophysiology. Figure \[ [19](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01080-y#Fig19)\]  presents Grad-CAM visualizations for Meningioma, Glioma, and Pituitary classes, showcasing the model’s analysis using representative MRI samples. The XAI-based approach effectively localized intra-axial regions with thick, irregular tumor boundaries and with central necrotic cores, which is a key MRI features indicative of tumor presence.

The findings of this study indicate that the proposed EL model, augmented with explainable AI techniques such as Grad-CAM, delivers high accuracy in classifying MRI images across different tumor types. Grad-CAM integration offers meaningful visual insights by highlighting the specific regions of MRI scans that most influence the model’s predictions. This level of explainability is essential, as it bridges the gap between complex AI decision-making and human interpretability, enabling clinicians to validate and better understand the model’s outputs. ## 5 Discussion

### 5.1 Slice-level analysis and patient-level decision making

In this study, model training is performed at the 2D slice level, while diagnostic decisions are derived at the patient level. It is acknowledged that MRI slices acquired from the same subject exhibit strong inter-slice correlation, particularly among adjacent axial planes. To prevent bias caused by such correlation, data partitioning was conducted strictly at the patient level, ensuring that all slices from a given subject were assigned exclusively to either the training, validation, or test set, thereby eliminating cross-set leakage.

Let \\(Si=\\{{s}\_{i1},{s}\_{i2},,\\dots,{s}\_{iNi},\\}\\) denote the set of slices belonging to the _i-th_ subject, where \\({N}\_{i}\\)​ represents the number of slices for that subject. For each slice \\({s}\_{ij}\\)​, the trained network produces a posterior probability vector \\({p}\_{ij}\\in{\\mathbb{R}}^{C}\\), where C denotes the number of diagnostic classes.

Patient-level prediction \\({\\widehat{y}}\_{i}\\)​ is obtained by aggregating slice-level probabilities using a confidence-weighted averaging scheme followed by majority voting:

$$\\widehat{{y}\_{i}}=\\text{arg}\\underset{c}{\\text{max}}\\left(\\frac{1}{{N}\_{i}}{\\sum}\_{j=1}^{{N}\_{i}}{p}\_{ij}^{\\left(c\\right)}\\right)$$

where \\({p}\_{ij}^{\\left(C\\right)}\\) denotes the predicted probability of class c for slice j. This aggregation strategy emphasizes consistent predictions across the full image volume while suppressing the influence of redundant or highly correlated slices.

Although 3D convolutional architectures can explicitly model volumetric spatial dependencies, a 2D slice-based paradigm was adopted due to limited availability of fully annotated volumetric datasets and computational constraints. This approach remains widely adopted in brain MRI analysis. To compensate for the lack of explicit inter-slice modeling, extensive data augmentation was applied exclusively to training slices, and patient-level aggregation was employed to enhance robustness and generalization.

Nevertheless, it is acknowledged that 2D models cannot fully exploit longitudinal contextual information across slices. Future work will explore 3D and hybrid 2.5D architectures to incorporate volumetric continuity and further improve patient-level diagnostic accuracy.

## 6 Conclusions and future work

This study presents a robust framework that integrates TL and ensemble learning for image-level multi-class classification of brain tumors using MRI images. This work proposes a deployment-aware heterogeneous ensemble of transfer-learned CNNs that jointly improves classification accuracy, cross-dataset generalization, and interpretability for multi-class brain tumor classification using MRI images. The proposed model effectively classifies brain tumors into four categories: glioma, meningioma, pituitary tumor, and no tumor, achieving a high accuracy of 99.15%. Six pre-trained TL CNNs VGG16, VGG19, InceptionV3, Xception, ResNet152, and DenseNet201 originally trained on the ImageNet dataset, were fine-tuned to adapt to the brain tumor classification task. Both training from scratch and transfer learning approaches were applied independently on each model using the pre-segmented Kaggle Brain MRI dataset to compare their performance. Confusion matrix analysis was used to evaluate and visualize the strengths and limitations of each architecture.

To further improve classification accuracy, ensemble learning was implemented using a weighted voting strategy. The four top-performing models VGG16, Xception, ResNet152, and DenseNet201 were selected through ensemble pruning to serve as individual classifiers. Based on extensive experimentation, a weighted voting mechanism, where each model’s weight corresponded to its accuracy, was used to combine their predictions effectively. Extensive experimentation confirmed that our ensemble method significantly outperformed individual models, achieving outstanding metrics: 99.285% accuracy, 98.619% precision, 99.558% recall, and 98.586% F1-score. Compared to individual transfer learning models, the proposed method improved accuracy by 0.1% to 5.25%, recall by 0.09% to 8.93%, and F1-score by approximately 0.3% to 5%. To validate model interpretability, we employed XAI technique such as Grad-CAM to visualize attention maps, highlighting tumor-affected regions in MRI scans. This explainability supports clinical transparency and aligns model predictions with medical reasoning, thereby improving its applicability in real-world healthcare settings. Although promising results are achieved, this study is limited to single-center data and basic geometric augmentations. Future work will explore more realistic disturbance models and multi-center datasets to better evaluate robustness under domain shifts and enhance clinical generalization.

Although the proposed framework operates on 2D MRI slices, the final diagnostic outcome is determined at the patient level. It is acknowledged that adjacent slices from the same subject exhibit a high degree of correlation. To prevent information leakage arising from this correlation, dataset partitioning was performed strictly at the patient level, ensuring that all slices belonging to a given subject appear exclusively in either the training, validation, or test sets. Slice-level classification is used as an intermediate representation to extract discriminative features from individual MRI slices. For patient-level diagnosis, predictions from all slices of a subject are aggregated using a majority-voting and confidence-weighted averaging strategy. This aggregation emphasizes consistent patterns across the full image volume and reduces the influence of redundant or highly similar slices.

While 3D CNN architectures can explicitly model volumetric spatial dependencies, a 2D slice-based approach was adopted in this study due to limited availability of fully annotated volumetric datasets and computational constraints, which remains a common practice in brain MRI analysis. To enhance robustness and generalization, data augmentation was applied exclusively to training slices, and patient-level aggregation was employed to mitigate slice redundancy. Nevertheless, we recognize that 2D methods do not fully capture inter-slice contextual information. Future work will investigate 3D and hybrid 2.5D architectures to better exploit volumetric continuity and further improve patient-level diagnostic performance.

The overarching goal of this work is to assist clinicians in accurately diagnosing brain tumor types while improving computational efficiency, reliability, and transparency. Nevertheless, there remains room for further development. Future work may explore alternative ensemble strategies, more refined weighting mechanisms, and the inclusion of additional tumor subtypes beyond the four classes studied. Moreover, the framework can be extended to 3D imaging data for better spatial feature extraction and diagnostic accuracy. The integration of transformer-based architectures could further elevate performance by leveraging their capability for sequential and contextual data processing. Ultimately, developing a real-time, user-friendly application would bridge the gap between research and clinical practice, making advanced diagnostic tools widely accessible.

metadata.title: A deep transfer learning and ensemble learning framework for brain tumor detection and classification in MRI images | Discover Artificial Intelligence | Springer Nature Link
metadata.dc.description: This study proposes a novel framework that integrates Transfer Learning (TL) and Ensemble Learning (EL) for multi-class classification of brain tumors using Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) images. The classification targets four categories: glioma, meningioma, pituitary tumor, and no tumor. Several state-of-the-art deep learning architectures from the VGG, Inception, ResNet, and DenseNet families were analyzed and compared. Based on their performance, six Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs)—VGG16, VGG19, InceptionV3, Xception, ResNet152, and DenseNet201—were selected for transfer learning to perform the classification task. To enhance classification accuracy, ensemble learning was applied using a weighted voting strategy, where the accuracy of each model served as its weight. The four top-performing models VGG16, Xception, ResNet152, and DenseNet201 were combined in this ensemble. To further interpret the model’s decisions, Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) technique, specifically Grad-CAM, was employed to highlight key regions in the MRI images that influenced the classification outcomes, thereby improving model transparency. The models were trained and evaluated on the publicly available BT-7023 dataset from Kaggle, consisting of 7,023 MRI images (5,712 for training and 1,311 for testing). Performance was assessed using accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. The proposed ensemble method achieved excellent results, with 99.28% accuracy, 98.62% precision, 99.56% recall, and a 98.58% F1-score. To verify the robustness of the approach, cross-dataset validation was conducted using an external dataset from Figshare. The proposed ensemble outperformed existing models on this dataset, achieving 98.80% accuracy. Overall, the ensemble framework demonstrated a 5%–13% performance improvement over existing methods, underscoring its effectiveness and reliability for early detection and classification of brain tumors. Additionally, the XAI-based analysis confirmed the model’s focus on clinically relevant tumor regions, enhancing interpretability and trustworthiness in medical applications.
